newsitem.title: GERMANY: ANALYSTS' COMMENTS ON REMARKS BY BUBA'S WELTEKE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS' COMMENTS ON REMARKS BY BUBA'S WELTEKE.

text.p: Following are comments from economists following remarks by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke who said Germany's central bank had already signalled it thought the dollar's 'correction' against the mark was completed at a rate of 1.70 marks.

Speaking on German radio, Welteke also said the Bundesbank was closely watching foreign exchange developments but said it had no exact date for intervening in currency markets. He also said it was "not appropriate to turn the interest rate screw" because of slow economic growth and high unemployment.
RALF KUGELSTADT, ECONOMIST AT UBS IN FRANKFURT

"In the past there has usually been a certain hierarchy of reaction to a falling mark, the central bank usually opts for intervention before changing interest rates. The domestic economy is an argument for not changing rates and experience shows intervention has not been that successful.

"The Bundesbank is worried about the momentum of the mark's fall more than about its absolute level. The bank is not interested in getting the dollar back down to 1.70 marks -- that would hurt company sentiment and dampen investment.

"Welteke using the word intervention does not affect the likelihood of whether it will happen or not. His comments do not necessarily reflect those of the Bundesbank's directorate and they contrast with what (Bundesbank chief economist Otmar) Issing said this week that the Bundesbank has to reconsider rates in the light of recent mark weakness.
"We don't expect an interest rate rise at the moment because of the relatively weak domestic economy."
UWE ANGENENDT, ECONOMIST AT BHF-BANK IN FRANKFURT

"The fact is that the Bundesbank has tied monetary policy to the development of the mark. The recent strengthening of the mark has taken some of the pressure off the Bundesbank. It has the option to set a combination of a variable-rate and a fixed-rate repo tender but the Bundesbank's scope for action is limited.

"Any big move in rates would have to be coordinated with other European central banks. Verbal intervention has only had a limited impact in the past and I don't expect Welteke's comments will impress the market for long. If the Bundesbank intervenes in the currency market it is likely to do so when the dollar is already weakening, to reinforce a move already started by the market."
